name: Climbazole

lead: Climbazole is an azole antifungal added to over-the-counter dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, sometimes alongside zinc pyrithione, to cut visible flaking and itching for a cleaner scalp. It targets the Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.

It belongs to the same class as ketoconazole and is described as inhibiting the fungal enzyme CYP51, which blocks ergosterol production in fungal membranes. Most published research concerns its presence in wastewater, rivers and fish. A 2001 clinical study of a climbazole shampoo for seborrheic scalp eczema is cited by Wikipedia, though no trial details were available.

paras: People use it as part of a regular anti-dandruff shampoo or conditioner routine, left on the scalp briefly before rinsing. It is bought over the counter, often as one active among several.

Local irritation such as redness and itching is reported. Grokipedia describes cosmetic-use limits in the EU and a 2024 ECHA flag for possible endocrine-disrupting properties; it is also reported as toxic to aquatic life.

angle.text: Climbazole is an antifungal in anti-dandruff products that goes after the yeast behind scalp flaking, so hair and shoulders look cleaner. It is in the same azole class as ketoconazole; the research in the sources is mostly environmental.

lead: Climbazole is a synthetic imidazole antifungal used as an active ingredient in over-the-counter anti-dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, and sometimes as a preservative.[1][2] It belongs to the same azole class as ketoconazole, clotrimazole and miconazole and is active against Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2]

Most published research found on climbazole concerns its detection and fate in the environment rather than clinical effect on the scalp: studies have measured it in wastewater, rivers and fish, and one has examined its ecotoxicity.[3][4][5] Wikipedia cites a 2001 clinical study of a climbazole dandruff shampoo for seborrheic scalp eczema, but no trial details were available for this article.[1]

paras: Climbazole is found in non-prescription shampoos for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, sometimes combined with zinc pyrithione or triclosan.[1] Grokipedia reports typical cosmetic concentrations of up to 2 percent in rinse-off products and 0.5 percent in leave-on products, where it may serve as both an antidandruff active and a preservative.[2]

Like other azoles, climbazole is described as inhibiting fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), disrupting synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of fungal cell membranes.[2] Reported minimum inhibitory concentrations against Malassezia species are low, and skin permeation is described as under 1 percent of the applied dose.[2]

Wikipedia notes that climbazole may cause local irritation such as redness, rash and itching.[1] Grokipedia reports negative mutagenicity tests and that EU regulators classified it as acceptable for cosmetic use within limits, while a 2024 ECHA assessment flagged potential endocrine-disrupting properties in the environment with human relevance still under evaluation; this account is AI-generated and should be treated cautiously.[2]
Environmental research has detected climbazole among personal-care product residues in wastewater and surface waters, and an ecotoxicity study examined its effects on aquatic organisms.[3][4][5][6]

No studies found beyond a single study cited on Wikipedia (a 2001 clinical study of a climbazole shampoo in seborrheic scalp eczema), whose results were not available for review.[1] Laboratory research has examined it as a hit in a screen for inhibitors of exosome release by prostate cancer cells; this is not a clinical use of shampoo ingredients.[7]
